overview: Promisia Healthcare is a small/micro-cap New Zealand aged care and retirement village operator listed on the NZX, running five integrated communities in Feilding, Christchurch and Cromwell comprising 401 care beds, 76 care suites/apartments and 156 independent-living villas (656 residents). The company is the product of a 2020 reverse-takeover-style transaction that turned a legacy dietary-supplement/arthritis-research shell (formerly Genestock/Promisia Integrative) into an aged-care operator, and it more than doubled its balance sheet in FY2025 via a debt- and vendor-loan-funded acquisition of two Cromwell villages. It has a 31 March fiscal year end and reports in NZD.

business_model.summary: Promisia earns recurring daily government-subsidised care fees for rest home/hospital/dementia beds, plus long-dated deferred management fees (DMF) crystallised on exit from occupation right agreements (ORAs) sold to independent-living villa and care-suite residents. ORA resident loans (interest-free, repayable on exit and re-issue to the next resident) are the dominant liability and effectively fund the underlying property; DMF is recognised straight-line over average expected occupancy (4.0-4.2 years for apartments, 7.0-8.1 years for villas). Fair-value revaluation gains on investment property (facilities/villages) flow through the P&L as non-cash "other income" and are the largest single swing factor in reported net profit.

revenue_streams.name: Care and village fees (rest home/hospital/dementia daily fees)
Deferred management fees (DMF) on ORA exits

business_model.customer_type: B2C - elderly residents and their families; government (Te Whatu Ora / Health NZ) as principal payer of residential care subsidy for care beds
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand only: Feilding (Ranfurly Manor, Nelson Street), Christchurch (Aldwins House), Cromwell (Golden View Lifestyle Village, Ripponburn Home & Hospital)

competitive_position.market_position: Sub-scale niche player (5 facilities, ~$107m portfolio value) versus the large-cap NZX retirement/aged-care operators (Ryman, Summerset, Oceania, Arvida) which have national networks of dozens of villages and vastly greater balance sheets and development pipelines. Promisia's stated strategy is to target medium/large stand-alone facilities in regional New Zealand that are too small to interest the majors, rather than compete head-on in the large metro new-build village model.

moat_factors.description: Aged-care facilities require Ministry of Health/Health NZ certification and ORA structures must comply with the Retirement Villages Act 2003, and new bed supply is constrained by funding settings - a barrier that protects incumbents generally, though it does not differentiate Promisia specifically

Existing licensed bed capacity is described by management as "increasingly valuable" given constrained new supply and rising demographic demand; established sites in regional centres (Feilding, Christchurch, Cromwell) are not easily replicated
Once a resident enters care or purchases an ORA, relocation is costly and disruptive, providing some revenue stability, though this is common across the sector, not company-specific

Small, regional brand recognition (Ranfurly Manor, Golden View, etc.) with no national brand power versus Ryman/Summerset; company is actively trying to build a consistent "Promisian" culture and quality reputation from a low base
Sub-scale versus large peers on procurement, corporate overhead and access to capital; management is only now consolidating suppliers and standardising systems across five sites

weaknesses: Very small scale (five facilities) limits operating leverage, negotiating power with suppliers/lenders, and diversification of geographic/regulatory risk
Micro-cap illiquidity - thin trading, small free float, concentrated register limits institutional interest
Historically weak occupancy at some sites (e.g., Nelson Street 58% and Ranfurly Manor care suites ~51% in FY2025) reflecting execution gaps versus larger, more professionally run peers
Heavier reliance on bank debt and vendor loans/convertible notes to fund growth than larger peers with broader capital market access
Single bank lending relationship (BNZ) concentrates refinancing risk

growth_drivers: Occupancy recovery/optimisation across the existing portfolio - Group care occupancy rose from 87% (Mar-25) to 94% (Mar-26), with a stated 95%+ target, directly lifting EBITDAF with minimal incremental capex
Full-year contribution and ongoing integration of the FY2025 Cromwell acquisition (Golden View, Ripponburn), which added ~$10.5m of annualised revenue and is now described as "fully integrated"
Nelson Street dementia wing conversion (completed June 2025) lifting a previously under-occupied facility to full capacity and improving care mix/revenue per bed
Growing deferred management fee base as villa/apartment ORA sales and resales increase, adding a higher-margin, capital-light revenue stream
New formal dividend policy from FY27 (20%-40% of Operating Free Cash Flow) signalling confidence in sustainable cash generation and potentially widening the shareholder base
Active pursuit of further earnings-accretive acquisitions of medium/large regional aged-care facilities in FY27, continuing the roll-up strategy
Debt restructure/consolidation with BNZ reducing the weighted average interest rate from 7.10% to 5.7% and lowering finance costs, improving free cash flow conversion

Secular demographic tailwind: NZ's over-65 population is projected to grow from ~900,000 to 1.3 million by 2040, with the sector facing a forecast shortfall of ~12,000 residential care beds by 2032, supporting long-run demand and asset values for existing licensed capacity
Development/expansion optionality at existing sites (e.g., increasing care capacity at Golden View, ~2.8-hectare development potential at Ripponburn)

business.description: Revenue and earnings are highly sensitive to occupancy; management explicitly flags any significant drop in occupancy as having a direct financial impact, and several facilities have shown volatile, sometimes very low, historical occupancy
Only five facilities across three regions; any single-site operational, reputational or regulatory problem (e.g., a failed certification audit) would be material to group results
Care and non-care staff are paid at the lower end of pay scales due to Te Whatu Ora underfunding, making recruitment and retention difficult sector-wide
Expansion and redevelopment of facilities carries construction and financing risk, and the company is "routinely investigating" further acquisitions with integration risk
Norovirus, COVID-19 and similar outbreaks pose ongoing operational and reputational risk in congregate-care settings

financial.description: Loan-to-value ratio of 31.8% (down from 42.9%) with all interest-bearing bank debt consolidated with a single lender, BNZ; $30.9m of borrowings mature within 1-2 years per the FY26 maturity table

$5.785m of BNZ debt remained unhedged at 31 March 2026 after interest rate swaps on $22.0m notional; a 1% rate rise would cost only ~$0.058m annually post-hedging, but refinancing at maturity carries rate risk

financial.risk: Convertible notes / vendor loan dilution and imputed interest
financial.description: Vendor loan and convertible note imputed interest expense rose to $1.252m in FY26 (from $0.456m); notes are a non-cash earnings drag and a future dilution/repayment obligation

financial.risk: Fair value gains are non-cash and can reverse
financial.description: A large share of reported profit (FY26 pre-tax profit $13.94m included an $11.65m non-cash fair value gain on investment property) depends on valuer assumptions on growth, occupancy and discount rates that could reverse in a downturn

regulatory.description: Residential care subsidy funding from Te Whatu Ora is below the level required to sustainably deliver high-quality care per management and industry commentary (NZ-wide ~$650m sector funding gap cited in press); any reduction or inadequate uplift materially affects margins
ORA structures must comply with the Retirement Villages Act 2003 and facilities are subject to Ministry of Health/Health NZ certification audits; tightening standards could raise compliance costs
A ministerial advisory group and Budget 2026 discussions on accommodation bonds and funding model changes create policy uncertainty that could reshape sector economics

macro.description: A sustained downturn in national/regional property markets could reduce demand for and pricing achieved on ORA unit/care-suite sales and resales, directly hitting DMF and new ORA gains
NZ interest rates affect both Promisia's own borrowing costs and prospective residents' ability to sell homes to fund ORA purchases
Aged care is labour-intensive; broader wage inflation pressures margins where government funding lags cost growth

execution.description: Promisia operates without a single CEO - a CFO (Francisco Rodriguez Ferrere) and COO (Graeme Dodd, joined May 2025) share responsibilities reporting directly to the Board; Tom Brankin is stepping down from his paid executive role at the 2026 AGM after a long history of driving acquisitions, a transition that removes an experienced dealmaker from day-to-day execution

Thomas Brankin and associated trust hold 42.74% of shares and Asset Management Limited holds 9.48% plus warrants; Tony Mortensen (Risk & Audit Committee Chair) is CEO of Asset Management Limited, a substantial shareholder, creating a related-party governance dynamic the Board has assessed but investors should note

The FY2025 Cromwell acquisition roughly doubled total assets in one transaction; successful integration (now largely complete per FY26 commentary) was and future acquisitions will remain a key execution risk for a management team of this size

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Structurally supportive long-term demand (NZ 65+ population growing from ~900k to 1.3m by 2040, sector facing a projected ~12,000-bed shortfall by 2032) but persistently strained by government funding levels that industry bodies (including the Aged Care Association, which Promisia engages with) say are below the cost of delivering quality care, producing an estimated ~$650m sector-wide funding gap and periodic facility closures/bed mothballing across the industry.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - care-bed revenue (government-subsidised, ~94% of Promisia's revenue) is relatively defensive and non-discretionary, but the DMF/ORA sales component is tied to the residential property market and household wealth, giving Promisia a secondary discretionary/cyclical exposure smaller peers with more villa-heavy mixes have to a greater degree.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - Promisia carries meaningful bank debt (LVR 31.8% at Mar-26) that is now largely swapped/hedged, reducing near-term sensitivity, but refinancing risk remains given the tight 1-2 year debt maturity concentration and reliance on a single lender (BNZ).
key_input_costs: Utilities/energy (company is installing solar at two sites to reduce exposure)

recent_developments.event: EMAC 1 Limited and EMAC 2 Limited (dormant subsidiaries) struck off the Companies Register; no impact on Group financials

Ongoing exercise of listed warrants (strike price $0.50, expiring 24 March 2027) has modestly expanded ordinary shares on issue beyond the 31 March 2026 balance of 52,729,550, e.g., 15,000 shares issued 5 June 2026 and further tranches through 2026, taking shares toward ~53.05m

FY26 annual results released: revenue $40.1m (+29% YoY), underlying EBITDAF $6.6m (+58% YoY, within the pre-announced $6.4-6.8m guided range), net profit $12.9m, NTA per share $1.09 (+38% YoY); Board introduced a formal cash-based dividend policy effective FY27 (20-40% of Operating Free Cash Flow, fully imputed)

Q4 FY26 operational update: Group care occupancy 94% in March 2026 (up from 92% in December quarter); Ranfurly Manor care suites 96% occupied/under contract versus 51% a year earlier; solar installations announced at Ranfurly Manor and Nelson Street (5-6 year payback)
Debbie McCusker appointed facility manager at Aldwins House, contributing to occupancy and reputation improvements
Ranfurly Manor passed its Health NZ certification audit; auditors noted quality of team and high resident/family satisfaction
Nelson Street's 20-bed dementia wing conversion completed (occupancy subsequently rose from 58% at Mar-25 to 96% at Mar-26, reaching full capacity); Graeme Dodd joined as Chief Operating Officer
Announced Tom Brankin will step down from his paid executive role at the 2026 AGM and continue only as a non-executive director; Craig Percy returned to independent (non-executive) director status

Transformational year: completed ~$33m acquisition of Golden View Lifestyle Village and Ripponburn Home & Hospital in Cromwell (Aug 2024, adding ~$10.5m annualised revenue), sold the Eileen Mary facility (Dannevirke), raised $4.725m of new equity, and executed a 500:1 consolidation of shares and warrants; total assets grew from $84.3m to $172.1m (more than doubled); all interest-bearing bank debt consolidated with BNZ, weighted average interest rate cut from 9.0% to 7.1%, LVR improved from 48.8% to 42.9%; a $6.6m non-cash bargain-purchase gain on the Cromwell acquisitions boosted reported FY25 profit

items.target: at least 20% growth to a minimum of $8.0 million
items.notes: Upgraded from an initial in-year FY26 guide; based on the existing portfolio (i.e., excludes any new acquisitions) and assumes group care occupancy maintained at or above 95% across the year

items.target: expected to materially improve versus FY26
items.vs_prior: new disclosure (OFCF newly defined as a KPI in FY26 report)
items.notes: OFCF = underlying EBITDAF less cash interest & required debt repayments, cash tax, and maintenance capex (depreciation used as proxy); underpins new dividend policy

items.target: Ordinary dividend of 20%-40% of Operating Free Cash Flow, fully imputed
items.vs_prior: new - first formal dividend policy adopted
items.notes: At Board discretion based on financial performance, position, funding requirements and growth opportunities; no dividend paid historically

items.vs_prior: raised trajectory (94% actual at Mar-26, up from 87% at Mar-25)
items.notes: Occupancy is described by the COO as "the oxygen that sustains our business"

items.target: actively working towards an earnings-accretive acquisition in FY27
items.notes: Consistent with strategy of acquiring medium/large integrated care and village facilities aligned with the existing operating model; also assessing development opportunities at existing sites

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Rhonda Sherriff and CFO Francisco Rodriguez Ferrere characterised FY26 as a year of broad-based operational and financial improvement built on a "reset and focused foundation-building" over the prior two years, citing occupancy gains, the completed BNZ debt consolidation, and CBRE revaluations confirming at least a 10% increase in value at every site. Management explicitly frames FY27 guidance as based on the existing portfolio only, with upside from any completed acquisition and from OFCF-funded dividends layered on top.

bull_case: Clear, credible earnings inflection: underlying EBITDAF up 58% in FY26 and guided up at least another 20% in FY27, driven by occupancy gains (87%→94%→95%+ target) that require little incremental capital

Balance sheet has been meaningfully de-risked - LVR down from 48.8% (FY24) to 31.8% (FY26), weighted average interest rate cut from 9.0% to 5.7%, single consolidated lender relationship with BNZ, and interest rate swaps now covering most of the debt book

Newly adopted, cash-flow-based dividend policy (20-40% of OFCF, fully imputed) signals management/Board confidence in earnings durability and could attract income-oriented investors to a stock that has never paid a dividend

Trades at a meaningful discount to net tangible assets (NTA of $1.09/share at Mar-26 versus a recent share price in the $0.60-0.75 range), offering asset-backed downside protection if valuations hold, with further upside from the demonstrated ability to buy assets below fair value (e.g., the $6.6m bargain-purchase gain on the FY25 Cromwell deal)

Structural demographic tailwind (NZ 65+ population growing to 1.3m by 2040, forecast 12,000-bed sector shortfall by 2032) supports long-run demand for existing licensed capacity and a credible ongoing roll-up strategy targeting under-optimised regional facilities
bear_case: Micro-cap scale and illiquidity - five facilities, ~$38m market cap, thin trading - mean company-specific operational shocks (a bad certification audit, a key facility manager departure, a local outbreak) can move the stock disproportionately and institutional demand is inherently limited

A large share of reported profit is non-cash and valuation-driven: FY26's $13.94m pre-tax profit included an $11.65m fair value gain on investment property, and FY25's included a $6.6m non-cash bargain-purchase gain; underlying cash generation (net operating cash flow of $6.4m in FY26) is much smaller than headline earnings and valuer assumptions could reverse in a downturn

Government aged-care funding remains, by management's and industry's own description, below the cost of sustainably delivering quality care, and staff pay sits at the lower end of scales - an unresolved structural sector risk that caps margin upside and pressures retention

Governance concentration: Thomas Brankin/family trust (42.7%) and Asset Management Limited (9.5% equity plus the majority of outstanding warrants) together control a large share of the register, and Asset Management's CEO chairs the Risk & Audit Committee - a related-party dynamic that, while disclosed and assessed by the Board, concentrates influence over capital allocation and governance

FY27 EBITDAF guidance of ≥$8m explicitly excludes any new acquisition, so the growth algorithm depends on continued occupancy gains that are already largely realised (94% actual vs. 95%+ target) and on management successfully sourcing, financing and integrating further earnings-accretive deals with a still-small executive team operating under a dual CFO/COO leadership model rather than a single CEO
